This topic concerns Docker container engineering and its role in packaging, distributing, and operating applications. Docker uses images to define application files and runtime defaults, containers to execute isolated processes, networks to provide connectivity, and volumes to preserve data. The exact implementation must be understood in relation to the topic title, its configuration, host dependencies, security boundaries, and operational lifecycle. Explain how Docker images are tagged, stored, retrieved, and distributed through registries. Cover image naming, registry hostnames, namespaces, tags, manifests, layers, digests, authentication, and push or pull behavior. Explain why mutable tags such as latest are not sufficient for reliable production traceability and why image digests provide immutable content identity. Include access control and credential protection. After completing this section, an engineer should be able to explain the concept in plain English, identify the Docker components involved, perform the relevant operation, inspect the resulting state, and recognize the risks of an incorrect implementation. ## 2. Docker Architecture and Technical Behavior Docker provides a workflow for building, distributing, and running containerized applications. The Docker CLI communicates with the Docker Engine API. The daemon manages images, containers, networks, and volumes. Containers execute application processes with isolation features provided by the host operating system. An image provides the filesystem and runtime configuration used to create a container. A container has its own runtime state and writable layer. Networks provide connectivity, and volumes or bind mounts provide access to persistent data. Registries distribute image content between development, CI, and deployment environments. For **Dependency Management — Repository and Artifact Management**, identify the relevant component, its inputs, its output, and the state it changes. Explain whether the operation happens during image construction, container startup, application execution, network communication, or data persistence. This distinction helps prevent confusion between an image configuration problem and a runtime failure. ## 3. Implementation Workflow 1. Verify Docker CLI and Engine availability with docker version and docker info. 2. Confirm the correct Docker context and target environment. 3. Inspect the image, container, network, volume, or configuration involved. 4. Review the required ports, filesystem paths, environment variables, permissions, and resource limits. 5. Apply the Dockerfile, CLI, Compose, or runtime configuration change. 6. Start or rebuild only the resources required for the operation. 7. Inspect the resulting state and capture logs or command output. 8. Run application-level validation rather than relying only on container status. 9. Record the image tag or digest and relevant configuration for repeatability. Docker commands can affect host resources and persistent data. Verify the selected context and resource names before removing containers, networks, images, or volumes. ## 4. Practical Docker Commands The following examples demonstrate relevant inspection and operational commands. Replace example names and image references with values from the actual environment. `ash id="dkr401" docker login registry.example.com docker tag payments-api:1.0 registry.example.com/team/payments-api:1.0 docker push registry.example.com/team/payments-api:1.0 docker pull registry.example.com/team/payments-api:1.0 docker image inspect registry.example.com/team/payments-api:1.0 ` Use commands that inspect state before commands that modify or remove resources. Do not expose registry credentials, secret environment variables, or private configuration in terminal recordings and CI logs. ## 5. Dockerfile Implementation Example A small Java application image can use a multi-stage build: `dockerfile id="dkr402" FROM maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-17 AS build WORKDIR /workspace COPY pom.xml . COPY src ./src RUN mvn -B clean package -DskipTests FROM eclipse-temurin:17-jre WORKDIR /app RUN useradd --system --uid 10001 appuser COPY --from=build /workspace/target/*.jar app.jar USER 10001 EXPOSE 8080 ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "/app/app.jar"] ` The build stage contains the Maven toolchain and creates the application package. The runtime stage contains only the Java runtime and application artifact. This reduces unnecessary build tooling in the final image. A production implementation should pin approved base-image versions, scan the result, validate the JAR selection, and consider image provenance and patching requirements. ## 6. Production DevOps Scenario Consider a Java payment service that must run consistently on developer machines, CI agents, and production hosts. The team creates a Dockerfile that builds the application and packages its runtime dependencies into an image. A Jenkins pipeline checks out a specific source commit, builds the image, runs automated tests, and performs a vulnerability scan. After successful validation, the pipeline publishes the image to a controlled registry. The image is identified by a versioned tag and immutable digest. The deployment process retrieves the approved image and starts the service with environment-specific configuration. Persistent transaction data is stored outside the disposable container layer. Network rules expose only the required application ports, and the container runs with restricted privileges. During a production incident, engineers inspect the container state, logs, resource consumption, network connectivity, and image digest. They can identify the exact image version and source revision instead of guessing which build is running. ## 7. Common Mistakes and Their Impact - Using an unpinned base image can introduce unexpected changes during rebuilds. - Copying the entire repository into the build context can increase build time and expose unnecessary files. - Embedding credentials in Dockerfile instructions can leave secrets in image layers. - Running every application process as root increases the impact of a container compromise. - Storing database files only in a container writable layer risks data loss. - Publishing the wrong host port can make a healthy application unreachable. - Assuming container startup means application readiness can cause dependent services to fail. - Using mutable image tags without recording digests weakens deployment traceability. - Ignoring resource limits can allow one container to exhaust host capacity. - Removing volumes during cleanup can permanently delete persistent application data. ## 8. Troubleshooting and Safe Recovery Start by identifying the affected resource and capturing its current state. Use docker ps -a to inspect container status, docker logs to inspect application output, and docker inspect to examine configuration and runtime state. For image-build failures, review the Dockerfile instruction, build context, .dockerignore rules, base image, and build output. For container startup failures, inspect the entrypoint, command, permissions, environment, and exit code. For connectivity failures, check port publishing, network membership, DNS, routing, and host firewall rules. For storage failures, inspect mounts, ownership, disk capacity, and volume state. Check daemon and host logs when container-level evidence does not explain the issue. Preserve logs and important data before removing or recreating resources. After applying a correction, verify both container health and actual application behavior. ## 9. Security and Production Best Practices Use trusted and maintained base images. Pin versions and record image digests for production releases. Scan images for known vulnerabilities and establish a patching process. Avoid embedding secrets in images or source repositories. Run application processes as non-root users where possible. Drop unnecessary Linux capabilities, avoid privileged containers, restrict host mounts, and protect access to the Docker daemon socket. Apply network segmentation and expose only required ports. Use volumes or external storage for important data. Configure resource limits, health checks, logging, and monitoring. Keep development, CI, and production configuration separate. Promote the same tested image between environments rather than rebuilding different images for each deployment target. ## 10. Verification and Completion Criteria The operation represented by **Dependency Management — Repository and Artifact Management** is complete only when the expected Docker state and application behavior are verified. Check that: - The correct Docker context and host were selected. - The intended image, container, network, or volume was used. - Configuration values and runtime permissions are correct. - The expected container process is running. - Application logs do not show unresolved startup failures. - Required network paths and service endpoints work. - Persistent data remains available after container recreation where required. - Resource limits and security settings match the intended policy. - The image tag or digest can be traced to the validated build. - The operation can be repeated using documented steps. ## 11. Practical Exercise Create a small application image using a Dockerfile. Build the image with a versioned tag and run it as a container with an explicitly published application port. Inspect the image and container configuration. Read application logs and verify the service endpoint. Introduce one controlled problem, such as an incorrect port mapping or invalid startup command. Observe the failure and collect evidence using Docker inspection and logs. Correct the configuration and recreate the container. Confirm that the application works and explain which configuration change resolved the issue. If the application requires persistent data, verify that the data remains available after replacing the container. ## 12. Interview and Engineering Understanding An engineer should be able to explain what **Dependency Management — Repository and Artifact Management** means, why Docker uses the relevant capability, which components participate, how the operation works, and how the result is verified. A strong practical answer describes the initial state, the exact Docker configuration or commands, the resulting image or container behavior, the evidence collected, and the production risks. Avoid simply listing commands. Explain what each command changes, which component performs the work, and how the final application behavior is confirmed.

This topic concerns Docker container engineering and its role in packaging, distributing, and operating applications. Docker uses images to define application files and runtime defaults, containers to execute isolated processes, networks to provide connectivity, and volumes to preserve data. The exact implementation must be understood in relation to the topic title, its configuration, host dependencies, security boundaries, and operational lifecycle. Explain the image build process and how Dockerfile instructions contribute to the resulting image. Cover FROM, WORKDIR, COPY, ADD where appropriate, RUN, ENV, ARG, EXPOSE, USER, CMD, and ENTRYPOINT according to the section's scope. Explain build context, .dockerignore, layer caching, multi-stage builds, reproducibility, image size, and the distinction between build-time arguments and runtime environment variables. Include the security risks of embedding secrets in image layers. After completing this section, an engineer should be able to explain the concept in plain English, identify the Docker components involved, perform the relevant operation, inspect the resulting state, and recognize the risks of an incorrect implementation. ## 2. Docker Architecture and Technical Behavior Docker provides a workflow for building, distributing, and running containerized applications. The Docker CLI communicates with the Docker Engine API. The daemon manages images, containers, networks, and volumes. Containers execute application processes with isolation features provided by the host operating system. An image provides the filesystem and runtime configuration used to create a container. A container has its own runtime state and writable layer. Networks provide connectivity, and volumes or bind mounts provide access to persistent data. Registries distribute image content between development, CI, and deployment environments. For **Dependency Scopes — Build Reproducibility**, identify the relevant component, its inputs, its output, and the state it changes. Explain whether the operation happens during image construction, container startup, application execution, network communication, or data persistence. This distinction helps prevent confusion between an image configuration problem and a runtime failure. ## 3. Implementation Workflow 1. Verify Docker CLI and Engine availability with docker version and docker info. 2. Confirm the correct Docker context and target environment. 3. Inspect the image, container, network, volume, or configuration involved. 4. Review the required ports, filesystem paths, environment variables, permissions, and resource limits. 5. Apply the Dockerfile, CLI, Compose, or runtime configuration change. 6. Start or rebuild only the resources required for the operation. 7. Inspect the resulting state and capture logs or command output. 8. Run application-level validation rather than relying only on container status. 9. Record the image tag or digest and relevant configuration for repeatability. Docker commands can affect host resources and persistent data. Verify the selected context and resource names before removing containers, networks, images, or volumes. ## 4. Practical Docker Commands The following examples demonstrate relevant inspection and operational commands. Replace example names and image references with values from the actual environment. `ash id="dkr401" docker version docker info docker build --no-cache -t payments-api:1.0 . docker image ls docker image inspect payments-api:1.0 docker history payments-api:1.0 ` Use commands that inspect state before commands that modify or remove resources. Do not expose registry credentials, secret environment variables, or private configuration in terminal recordings and CI logs. ## 5. Dockerfile Implementation Example A small Java application image can use a multi-stage build: `dockerfile id="dkr402" FROM maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-17 AS build WORKDIR /workspace COPY pom.xml . COPY src ./src RUN mvn -B clean package -DskipTests FROM eclipse-temurin:17-jre WORKDIR /app RUN useradd --system --uid 10001 appuser COPY --from=build /workspace/target/*.jar app.jar USER 10001 EXPOSE 8080 ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "/app/app.jar"] ` The build stage contains the Maven toolchain and creates the application package. The runtime stage contains only the Java runtime and application artifact. This reduces unnecessary build tooling in the final image. A production implementation should pin approved base-image versions, scan the result, validate the JAR selection, and consider image provenance and patching requirements. ## 6. Production DevOps Scenario Consider a Java payment service that must run consistently on developer machines, CI agents, and production hosts. The team creates a Dockerfile that builds the application and packages its runtime dependencies into an image. A Jenkins pipeline checks out a specific source commit, builds the image, runs automated tests, and performs a vulnerability scan. After successful validation, the pipeline publishes the image to a controlled registry. The image is identified by a versioned tag and immutable digest. The deployment process retrieves the approved image and starts the service with environment-specific configuration. Persistent transaction data is stored outside the disposable container layer. Network rules expose only the required application ports, and the container runs with restricted privileges. During a production incident, engineers inspect the container state, logs, resource consumption, network connectivity, and image digest. They can identify the exact image version and source revision instead of guessing which build is running. ## 7. Common Mistakes and Their Impact - Using an unpinned base image can introduce unexpected changes during rebuilds. - Copying the entire repository into the build context can increase build time and expose unnecessary files. - Embedding credentials in Dockerfile instructions can leave secrets in image layers. - Running every application process as root increases the impact of a container compromise. - Storing database files only in a container writable layer risks data loss. - Publishing the wrong host port can make a healthy application unreachable. - Assuming container startup means application readiness can cause dependent services to fail. - Using mutable image tags without recording digests weakens deployment traceability. - Ignoring resource limits can allow one container to exhaust host capacity. - Removing volumes during cleanup can permanently delete persistent application data. ## 8. Troubleshooting and Safe Recovery Start by identifying the affected resource and capturing its current state. Use docker ps -a to inspect container status, docker logs to inspect application output, and docker inspect to examine configuration and runtime state. For image-build failures, review the Dockerfile instruction, build context, .dockerignore rules, base image, and build output. For container startup failures, inspect the entrypoint, command, permissions, environment, and exit code. For connectivity failures, check port publishing, network membership, DNS, routing, and host firewall rules. For storage failures, inspect mounts, ownership, disk capacity, and volume state. Check daemon and host logs when container-level evidence does not explain the issue. Preserve logs and important data before removing or recreating resources. After applying a correction, verify both container health and actual application behavior. ## 9. Security and Production Best Practices Use trusted and maintained base images. Pin versions and record image digests for production releases. Scan images for known vulnerabilities and establish a patching process. Avoid embedding secrets in images or source repositories. Run application processes as non-root users where possible. Drop unnecessary Linux capabilities, avoid privileged containers, restrict host mounts, and protect access to the Docker daemon socket. Apply network segmentation and expose only required ports. Use volumes or external storage for important data. Configure resource limits, health checks, logging, and monitoring. Keep development, CI, and production configuration separate. Promote the same tested image between environments rather than rebuilding different images for each deployment target. ## 10. Verification and Completion Criteria The operation represented by **Dependency Scopes — Build Reproducibility** is complete only when the expected Docker state and application behavior are verified. Check that: - The correct Docker context and host were selected. - The intended image, container, network, or volume was used. - Configuration values and runtime permissions are correct. - The expected container process is running. - Application logs do not show unresolved startup failures. - Required network paths and service endpoints work. - Persistent data remains available after container recreation where required. - Resource limits and security settings match the intended policy. - The image tag or digest can be traced to the validated build. - The operation can be repeated using documented steps. ## 11. Practical Exercise Create a small application image using a Dockerfile. Build the image with a versioned tag and run it as a container with an explicitly published application port. Inspect the image and container configuration. Read application logs and verify the service endpoint. Introduce one controlled problem, such as an incorrect port mapping or invalid startup command. Observe the failure and collect evidence using Docker inspection and logs. Correct the configuration and recreate the container. Confirm that the application works and explain which configuration change resolved the issue. If the application requires persistent data, verify that the data remains available after replacing the container. ## 12. Interview and Engineering Understanding An engineer should be able to explain what **Dependency Scopes — Build Reproducibility** means, why Docker uses the relevant capability, which components participate, how the operation works, and how the result is verified. A strong practical answer describes the initial state, the exact Docker configuration or commands, the resulting image or container behavior, the evidence collected, and the production risks. Avoid simply listing commands. Explain what each command changes, which component performs the work, and how the final application behavior is confirmed.

The daemon manages images, containers, networks, and volumes. Containers execute application processes with isolation features provided by the host operating system. For **Phases and Goals — Build Tool Fundamentals**, identify the relevant component, its inputs, its output, and the state it changes. Verify Docker CLI and Engine availability with docker version and docker info. 2. Confirm the correct Docker context and target environment. 3. Inspect the image, container, network, volume, or configuration involved. 4. Review the required ports, filesystem paths, environment variables, permissions, and resource limits. 5. Apply the Dockerfile, CLI, Compose, or runtime configuration change. 6. Start or rebuild only the resources required for the operation. 7. Inspect the resulting state and capture logs or command output. 8. Run application-level validation rather than relying only on container status. 9. Record the image tag or digest and relevant configuration for repeatability. Docker commands can affect host resources and persistent data. This topic concerns Docker container engineering and its role in packaging, distributing, and operating applications. Docker uses images to define application files and runtime defaults, containers to execute isolated processes, networks to provide connectivity, and volumes to preserve data. The exact implementation must be understood in relation to the topic title, its configuration, host dependencies, security boundaries, and operational lifecycle. Explain the image build process and how Dockerfile instructions contribute to the resulting image. Cover FROM, WORKDIR, COPY, ADD where appropriate, RUN, ENV, ARG, EXPOSE, USER, CMD, and ENTRYPOINT according to the section's scope. Explain build context, .dockerignore, layer caching, multi-stage builds, reproducibility, image size, and the distinction between build-time arguments and runtime environment variables. Include the security risks of embedding secrets in image layers. After completing this section, an engineer should be able to explain the concept in plain English, identify the Docker components involved, perform the relevant operation, inspect the resulting state, and recognize the risks of an incorrect implementation. ## 2. Docker Architecture and Technical Behavior Docker provides a workflow for building, distributing, and running containerized applications. The Docker CLI communicates with the Docker Engine API. The daemon manages images, containers, networks, and volumes. Containers execute application processes with isolation features provided by the host operating system. An image provides the filesystem and runtime configuration used to create a container. A container has its own runtime state and writable layer. Networks provide connectivity, and volumes or bind mounts provide access to persistent data. Registries distribute image content between development, CI, and deployment environments. For **Maven Plugins — Hands-on Build Implementation**, identify the relevant component, its inputs, its output, and the state it changes. Explain whether the operation happens during image construction, container startup, application execution, network communication, or data persistence. This distinction helps prevent confusion between an image configuration problem and a runtime failure. ## 3. Implementation Workflow 1. Verify Docker CLI and Engine availability with docker version and docker info. 2. Confirm the correct Docker context and target environment. 3. Inspect the image, container, network, volume, or configuration involved. 4. Review the required ports, filesystem paths, environment variables, permissions, and resource limits. 5. Apply the Dockerfile, CLI, Compose, or runtime configuration change. 6. Start or rebuild only the resources required for the operation. 7. Inspect the resulting state and capture logs or command output. 8. Run application-level validation rather than relying only on container status. 9. Record the image tag or digest and relevant configuration for repeatability. Docker commands can affect host resources and persistent data. Verify the selected context and resource names before removing containers, networks, images, or volumes. ## 4. Practical Docker Commands The following examples demonstrate relevant inspection and operational commands. Replace example names and image references with values from the actual environment. `ash id="dkr401" docker version docker info docker build --no-cache -t payments-api:1.0 . docker image ls docker image inspect payments-api:1.0 docker history payments-api:1.0 ` Use commands that inspect state before commands that modify or remove resources. Do not expose registry credentials, secret environment variables, or private configuration in terminal recordings and CI logs. ## 5. Dockerfile Implementation Example A small Java application image can use a multi-stage build: `dockerfile id="dkr402" FROM maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-17 AS build WORKDIR /workspace COPY pom.xml . COPY src ./src RUN mvn -B clean package -DskipTests FROM eclipse-temurin:17-jre WORKDIR /app RUN useradd --system --uid 10001 appuser COPY --from=build /workspace/target/*.jar app.jar USER 10001 EXPOSE 8080 ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "/app/app.jar"] ` The build stage contains the Maven toolchain and creates the application package. The runtime stage contains only the Java runtime and application artifact. This reduces unnecessary build tooling in the final image. A production implementation should pin approved base-image versions, scan the result, validate the JAR selection, and consider image provenance and patching requirements. ## 6. Production DevOps Scenario Consider a Java payment service that must run consistently on developer machines, CI agents, and production hosts. The team creates a Dockerfile that builds the application and packages its runtime dependencies into an image. A Jenkins pipeline checks out a specific source commit, builds the image, runs automated tests, and performs a vulnerability scan. After successful validation, the pipeline publishes the image to a controlled registry. The image is identified by a versioned tag and immutable digest. The deployment process retrieves the approved image and starts the service with environment-specific configuration. Persistent transaction data is stored outside the disposable container layer. Network rules expose only the required application ports, and the container runs with restricted privileges. During a production incident, engineers inspect the container state, logs, resource consumption, network connectivity, and image digest. They can identify the exact image version and source revision instead of guessing which build is running. ## 7. Common Mistakes and Their Impact - Using an unpinned base image can introduce unexpected changes during rebuilds. - Copying the entire repository into the build context can increase build time and expose unnecessary files. - Embedding credentials in Dockerfile instructions can leave secrets in image layers. - Running every application process as root increases the impact of a container compromise. - Storing database files only in a container writable layer risks data loss. - Publishing the wrong host port can make a healthy application unreachable. - Assuming container startup means application readiness can cause dependent services to fail. - Using mutable image tags without recording digests weakens deployment traceability. - Ignoring resource limits can allow one container to exhaust host capacity. - Removing volumes during cleanup can permanently delete persistent application data. ## 8. Troubleshooting and Safe Recovery Start by identifying the affected resource and capturing its current state. Use docker ps -a to inspect container status, docker logs to inspect application output, and docker inspect to examine configuration and runtime state. For image-build failures, review the Dockerfile instruction, build context, .dockerignore rules, base image, and build output. For container startup failures, inspect the entrypoint, command, permissions, environment, and exit code. For connectivity failures, check port publishing, network membership, DNS, routing, and host firewall rules. For storage failures, inspect mounts, ownership, disk capacity, and volume state. Check daemon and host logs when container-level evidence does not explain the issue. Preserve logs and important data before removing or recreating resources. After applying a correction, verify both container health and actual application behavior. ## 9. Security and Production Best Practices Use trusted and maintained base images. Pin versions and record image digests for production releases. Scan images for known vulnerabilities and establish a patching process. Avoid embedding secrets in images or source repositories. Run application processes as non-root users where possible. Drop unnecessary Linux capabilities, avoid privileged containers, restrict host mounts, and protect access to the Docker daemon socket. Apply network segmentation and expose only required ports. Use volumes or external storage for important data. Configure resource limits, health checks, logging, and monitoring. Keep development, CI, and production configuration separate. Promote the same tested image between environments rather than rebuilding different images for each deployment target. ## 10. Verification and Completion Criteria The operation represented by **Maven Plugins — Hands-on Build Implementation** is complete only when the expected Docker state and application behavior are verified. Check that: - The correct Docker context and host were selected. - The intended image, container, network, or volume was used. - Configuration values and runtime permissions are correct. - The expected container process is running. - Application logs do not show unresolved startup failures. - Required network paths and service endpoints work. - Persistent data remains available after container recreation where required. - Resource limits and security settings match the intended policy. - The image tag or digest can be traced to the validated build. - The operation can be repeated using documented steps. ## 11. Practical Exercise Create a small application image using a Dockerfile. Build the image with a versioned tag and run it as a container with an explicitly published application port. Inspect the image and container configuration. Read application logs and verify the service endpoint. Introduce one controlled problem, such as an incorrect port mapping or invalid startup command. Observe the failure and collect evidence using Docker inspection and logs. Correct the configuration and recreate the container. Confirm that the application works and explain which configuration change resolved the issue. If the application requires persistent data, verify that the data remains available after replacing the container. ## 12. A strong practical answer describes the initial state, the exact Docker configuration or commands, the resulting image or container behavior, the evidence collected, and the production risks. Avoid simply listing commands. Explain what each command changes, which component performs the work, and how the final application behavior is confirmed.

Explanation and Learning Objective This section belongs to **Spring Boot Packaging** in Stage 04: Docker Container Engineering. Explain a structured troubleshooting workflow. Begin with docker ps -a, docker inspect, docker logs, and the container exit code. Inspect the image, entrypoint, command, environment, mounts, network, and resource configuration. Check daemon logs and host capacity when container-level evidence is insufficient. Classify the problem before taking action, preserve logs, and avoid deleting containers or volumes before important evidence and data are secured. After completing this section, an engineer should be able to explain the concept in plain English, identify the Docker components involved, perform the relevant operation, inspect the resulting state, and recognize the risks of an incorrect implementation. ## 2. Docker Architecture and Technical Behavior Docker provides a workflow for building, distributing, and running containerized applications. The Docker CLI communicates with the Docker Engine API. The daemon manages images, containers, networks, and volumes. Containers execute application processes with isolation features provided by the host operating system. An image provides the filesystem and runtime configuration used to create a container. A container has its own runtime state and writable layer. Networks provide connectivity, and volumes or bind mounts provide access to persistent data. Registries distribute image content between development, CI, and deployment environments. For **Spring Boot Packaging — Troubleshooting and Diagnostics**, identify the relevant component, its inputs, its output, and the state it changes. Explain whether the operation happens during image construction, container startup, application execution, network communication, or data persistence. This distinction helps prevent confusion between an image configuration problem and a runtime failure. ## 3. Implementation Workflow 1. Verify Docker CLI and Engine availability with docker version and docker info. 2. Confirm the correct Docker context and target environment. 3. Inspect the image, container, network, volume, or configuration involved. 4. Review the required ports, filesystem paths, environment variables, permissions, and resource limits. 5. Apply the Dockerfile, CLI, Compose, or runtime configuration change. 6. Start or rebuild only the resources required for the operation. 7. Inspect the resulting state and capture logs or command output. 8. Run application-level validation rather than relying only on container status. 9. Record the image tag or digest and relevant configuration for repeatability. Docker commands can affect host resources and persistent data. Content: # Testing Fundamentals — Testing Strategy and Fundamentals ## 1. Explanation and Learning Objective This section belongs to **Testing Fundamentals** in Stage 05: Kubernetes Container Orchestration. Kubernetes manages containerized applications through a declarative API and a set of controllers that continuously reconcile actual cluster state with the desired state declared in resource specifications. The relevant components may include Pods, workload controllers, Services, networking, storage, configuration resources, scheduling, security controls, and observability systems. The engineering objective is to run applications reliably, securely, and predictably across a cluster. Define the Kubernetes concept represented by this section and explain the problem it solves. Describe where it fits in a cluster and application lifecycle. Identify the relevant API resource, controller, node component, or external integration. Explain technical terms in beginner-friendly language and distinguish Kubernetes orchestration from the responsibility of the application running inside a container. After completing this section, an engineer should be able to explain the concept in plain English, identify the Kubernetes resources and components involved, perform the relevant operation, inspect cluster state, and recognize the risks of an incorrect implementation. ## 2. Kubernetes Technical Architecture and Behavior Kubernetes uses a declarative operating model. An engineer declares the desired state in API resources, and Kubernetes controllers continuously work to reconcile the actual cluster state with that desired state. The API server is the main entry point for cluster operations. Authentication, authorization, and admission controls determine whether a request can be accepted. etcd stores cluster state. Controllers monitor resources and create or update dependent objects. The scheduler assigns unscheduled Pods to suitable nodes. The kubelet on each worker node works with the container runtime to ensure assigned workloads run as specified. For **Testing Fundamentals — Testing Strategy and Fundamentals**, identify the API resource, controller, node component, or external integration responsible for the behavior. Explain what state is submitted, what reconciliation takes place, and how the result can be observed. Do not assume that a successful kubectl apply means the application is healthy. API acceptance, scheduling, container startup, readiness, and application availability are separate conditions. ## 3. Implementation Workflow 1. Confirm the current Kubernetes context with kubectl config current-context. 2. Select and verify the correct namespace. 3. Inspect the relevant resources before changing anything. 4. Review the manifest fields, image reference, labels, selectors, resources, and permissions. 5. Apply the required configuration using a reviewed manifest or approved deployment process. 6. Observe controller reconciliation and Pod scheduling. 7. Inspect Pod conditions, container state, events, and logs. 8. Verify networking, storage, and application readiness where required. 9. Record the manifest revision, image digest, and resulting workload state. Use namespaces and explicit resource names to avoid changing the wrong environment. Before deleting or replacing resources, determine whether they own persistent data or production traffic. ## 4. Practical Kubernetes Commands The following commands provide relevant inspection and operational examples. Replace placeholder resource names and namespaces with actual values. `ash id="k8s501" kubectl cluster-info kubectl get nodes -o wide kubectl get namespaces kubectl get pods -A kubectl get services -A kubectl get events -A --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp ` Commands that modify resources should be executed only after checking the active context and reviewing the target manifest. Avoid copying production credentials or secret values into terminal history. ## 5. Kubernetes Workload Example The following Deployment demonstrates a basic stateless application workload: `yaml id="k8s502" apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: payments-api namespace: production spec: replicas: 3 selector: matchLabels: app: payments-api template: metadata: labels: app: payments-api spec: containers: - name: application image: registry.example.com/payments-api:1.4.0 ports: - name: http containerPort: 8080 resources: requests: cpu: "250m" memory: "256Mi" limits: cpu: "1000m" memory: "512Mi" readinessProbe: httpGet: path: /health port: http initialDelaySeconds: 10 periodSeconds: 5 livenessProbe: httpGet: path: /health port: http initialDelaySeconds: 30 periodSeconds: 10 ` The Deployment declares three desired replicas. Its controller creates and maintains the Pods. Resource requests help the scheduler select suitable nodes, while limits constrain container consumption. Readiness determines whether a Pod should receive Service traffic. The example must be adapted to the actual application health endpoints and resource profile. ## 6. Production DevOps Scenario Consider a Java payment application deployed to a Kubernetes cluster. The development team stores its source code and Kubernetes manifests in version control. A CI pipeline builds and tests the application, scans the image, and publishes an immutable image digest to a registry. A delivery process updates the Deployment manifest to reference the approved image. Kubernetes accepts the updated desired state and begins a rolling update. The scheduler selects nodes with sufficient available resources. Kubelets start the containers, and readiness probes determine when the new Pods can receive traffic. The Service routes requests to ready endpoints. Monitoring records application latency, error rates, Pod restarts, CPU usage, memory usage, and node health. If the new version fails readiness or application validation, the delivery process stops or rolls back according to the deployment policy. The team records the source commit, image digest, manifest revision, deployment time, and validation result. This makes it possible to identify exactly which application version is running during an incident. ## 7. Common Mistakes and Their Impact - Applying manifests to the wrong Kubernetes context can change an unintended cluster. - Incorrect labels or selectors can leave Services without matching Pod endpoints. - Missing resource requests can make scheduling unpredictable under resource pressure. - Excessively low memory limits can cause containers to be terminated with OOMKilled. - Incorrect readiness probes can prevent healthy applications from receiving traffic. - Incorrect liveness probes can repeatedly restart an application that is still recovering. - Using mutable image tags weakens deployment traceability. - Broad RBAC permissions increase the impact of compromised identities. - Deleting PersistentVolumeClaims without understanding reclaim behavior can cause data loss. - Assuming Pod creation means application readiness can cause outages. - Ignoring namespace boundaries can lead to incorrect resource inspection or modification. ## 8. Troubleshooting and Safe Recovery Start by confirming the active context, namespace, resource name, and timestamp of the failure. Inspect resource state using kubectl get and kubectl describe. Review events for scheduling failures, image-pull errors, mount failures, probe failures, and node pressure. For a Pending Pod, inspect scheduling events, node capacity, resource requests, taints, tolerations, and affinity. For ImagePullBackOff, verify the image reference, registry availability, and image-pull credentials. For CrashLoopBackOff, inspect current and previous container logs, exit codes, commands, configuration, and resource limits. For service connectivity problems, inspect Service selectors, EndpointSlices, DNS, network policies, and the cluster network implementation. For storage failures, inspect PVC binding, PV state, CSI components, access modes, and mount events. Apply the smallest safe correction. Preserve evidence before deleting Pods or changing shared resources. Verify the recovery through resource conditions and an actual application request. ## 9. Security and Production Best Practices Use least-privilege RBAC for human users and service accounts. Avoid granting cluster-admin access to application workloads. Protect Secrets through encryption at rest, restrictive access, controlled rotation, and secure external secret integration where required. Use trusted and scanned container images. Run containers as non-root where possible, drop unnecessary Linux capabilities, restrict privilege escalation, and use appropriate seccomp and Pod security controls. Apply network policies when supported by the cluster network plugin. Set realistic resource requests and limits. Configure readiness, liveness, and startup probes according to application behavior. Use controlled rollout strategies, topology-aware scheduling, disruption budgets, and capacity planning for important services. Back up stateful data and test restoration. Monitor control-plane access, node health, Pod restarts, application SLOs, storage capacity, and cluster resource pressure. Keep cluster versions, add-ons, and workload manifests within supported compatibility ranges. ## 10. Verification and Completion Criteria The operation represented by **Testing Fundamentals — Testing Strategy and Fundamentals** is complete only when the declared and actual cluster states are consistent and the application behavior has been verified. Check that: - The intended cluster context and namespace were used. - The correct API resources were created or updated. - Selectors and labels connect the intended resources. - Pods are scheduled and containers start successfully. - Readiness and health checks report the expected state. - Services expose the intended endpoints. - Required storage is mounted and persistent data is safe. - Resource requests, limits, and security settings match policy. - Events and logs contain no unresolved operational failures. - The application responds correctly through its intended access path. - The image and manifest revisions can be traced to the approved release. ## 11. Practical Exercise Create a namespace and deploy a small application using a Deployment manifest. Add a Service that selects the application Pods. Inspect the Deployment, ReplicaSet, Pods, Service, and endpoints. Change the image reference to an invalid image and observe the resulting image-pull failure. Use kubectl describe and events to identify the reason. Restore the valid image reference and observe the successful rollout. Test the application through the Service. Explain the difference between a Pod being created, a container running, a Pod becoming ready, and the application successfully responding to a request. ## 12. Kubernetes manages containerized applications through a declarative API and a set of controllers that continuously reconcile actual cluster state with the desired state declared in resource specifications. The relevant components may include Pods, workload controllers, Services, networking, storage, configuration resources, scheduling, security controls, and observability systems. The engineering objective is to run applications reliably, securely, and predictably across a cluster. Define the Kubernetes concept represented by this section and explain the problem it solves. Describe where it fits in a cluster and application lifecycle. Identify the relevant API resource, controller, node component, or external integration. Explain technical terms in beginner-friendly language and distinguish Kubernetes orchestration from the responsibility of the application running inside a container. After completing this section, an engineer should be able to explain the concept in plain English, identify the Kubernetes resources and components involved, perform the relevant operation, inspect cluster state, and recognize the risks of an incorrect implementation. ## 2. Kubernetes Technical Architecture and Behavior Kubernetes uses a declarative operating model. An engineer declares the desired state in API resources, and Kubernetes controllers continuously work to reconcile the actual cluster state with that desired state. The API server is the main entry point for cluster operations. Authentication, authorization, and admission controls determine whether a request can be accepted. etcd stores cluster state. Controllers monitor resources and create or update dependent objects. The scheduler assigns unscheduled Pods to suitable nodes. The kubelet on each worker node works with the container runtime to ensure assigned workloads run as specified. For **Testing Fundamentals — Framework Architecture**, identify the API resource, controller, node component, or external integration responsible for the behavior. Explain what state is submitted, what reconciliation takes place, and how the result can be observed. Do not assume that a successful kubectl apply means the application is healthy. API acceptance, scheduling, container startup, readiness, and application availability are separate conditions. ## 3. Implementation Workflow 1. Confirm the current Kubernetes context with kubectl config current-context. 2. Select and verify the correct namespace. 3. Inspect the relevant resources before changing anything. 4. Review the manifest fields, image reference, labels, selectors, resources, and permissions. 5. Apply the required configuration using a reviewed manifest or approved deployment process. 6. Observe controller reconciliation and Pod scheduling. 7. Inspect Pod conditions, container state, events, and logs. 8. Verify networking, storage, and application readiness where required. 9. Record the manifest revision, image digest, and resulting workload state. Use namespaces and explicit resource names to avoid changing the wrong environment. Before deleting or replacing resources, determine whether they own persistent data or production traffic. ## 4. Practical Kubernetes Commands The following commands provide relevant inspection and operational examples. Replace placeholder resource names and namespaces with actual values. `ash id="k8s501" kubectl cluster-info kubectl get nodes -o wide kubectl get namespaces kubectl get pods -A kubectl get services -A kubectl get events -A --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp ` Commands that modify resources should be executed only after checking the active context and reviewing the target manifest. Avoid copying production credentials or secret values into terminal history. ## 5. Kubernetes Workload Example The following Deployment demonstrates a basic stateless application workload: `yaml id="k8s502" apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: payments-api namespace: production spec: replicas: 3 selector: matchLabels: app: payments-api template: metadata: labels: app: payments-api spec: containers: - name: application image: registry.example.com/payments-api:1.4.0 ports: - name: http containerPort: 8080 resources: requests: cpu: "250m" memory: "256Mi" limits: cpu: "1000m" memory: "512Mi" readinessProbe: httpGet: path: /health port: http initialDelaySeconds: 10 periodSeconds: 5 livenessProbe: httpGet: path: /health port: http initialDelaySeconds: 30 periodSeconds: 10 ` The Deployment declares three desired replicas. Its controller creates and maintains the Pods. Resource requests help the scheduler select suitable nodes, while limits constrain container consumption. Readiness determines whether a Pod should receive Service traffic. The example must be adapted to the actual application health endpoints and resource profile. ## 6. Production DevOps Scenario Consider a Java payment application deployed to a Kubernetes cluster. The development team stores its source code and Kubernetes manifests in version control. A CI pipeline builds and tests the application, scans the image, and publishes an immutable image digest to a registry. A delivery process updates the Deployment manifest to reference the approved image. Kubernetes accepts the updated desired state and begins a rolling update. The scheduler selects nodes with sufficient available resources. Kubelets start the containers, and readiness probes determine when the new Pods can receive traffic. The Service routes requests to ready endpoints. Monitoring records application latency, error rates, Pod restarts, CPU usage, memory usage, and node health. For ImagePullBackOff, verify the image reference, registry availability, and image-pull credentials. For CrashLoopBackOff, inspect current and previous container logs, exit codes, commands, configuration, and resource limits. For service connectivity problems, inspect Service selectors, EndpointSlices, DNS, network policies, and the cluster network implementation. For storage failures, inspect PVC binding, PV state, CSI components, access modes, and mount events. Apply the smallest safe correction. Preserve evidence before deleting Pods or changing shared resources. Verify the recovery through resource conditions and an actual application request. ## 9. Protect Secrets through encryption at rest, restrictive access, controlled rotation, and secure external secret integration where required. Use trusted and scanned container images. Run containers as non-root where possible, drop unnecessary Linux capabilities, restrict privilege escalation, and use appropriate seccomp and Pod security controls. Apply network policies when supported by the cluster network plugin. Set realistic resource requests and limits. Configure readiness, liveness, and startup probes according to application behavior. Use controlled rollout strategies, topology-aware scheduling, disruption budgets, and capacity planning for important services. Back up stateful data and test restoration. Monitor control-plane access, node health, Pod restarts, application SLOs, storage capacity, and cluster resource pressure. Keep cluster versions, add-ons, and workload manifests within supported compatibility ranges. ## 10. Check that: - The intended cluster context and namespace were used. - The correct API resources were created or updated. - Selectors and labels connect the intended resources. - Pods are scheduled and containers start successfully. - Readiness and health checks report the expected state. - Services expose the intended endpoints. - Required storage is mounted and persistent data is safe. - Resource requests, limits, and security settings match policy. - Events and logs contain no unresolved operational failures. - The application responds correctly through its intended access path. - The image and manifest revisions can be traced to the approved release. ## 11. A CI pipeline builds and tests the application, scans the image, and publishes an immutable image digest to a registry. A delivery process updates the Deployment manifest to reference the approved image. Kubernetes accepts the updated desired state and begins a rolling update. The scheduler selects nodes with sufficient available resources. Kubelets start the containers, and readiness probes determine when the new Pods can receive traffic. The Service routes requests to ready endpoints. Monitoring records application latency, error rates, Pod restarts, CPU usage, memory usage, and node health. For ImagePullBackOff, verify the image reference, registry availability, and image-pull credentials. For CrashLoopBackOff, inspect current and previous container logs, exit codes, commands, configuration, and resource limits. Content: # JUnit 5 Architecture — Testing Strategy and Fundamentals ## Learning Objective JUnit 5 is the modern Java testing platform used to write, discover, and execute automated tests. It is not a single library. JUnit 5 consists of JUnit Platform, JUnit Jupiter, and JUnit Vintage. Understanding these parts helps developers configure test execution correctly in Maven, Gradle, IDEs, and CI pipelines. ## Core Architecture JUnit Platform provides the foundation for launching testing frameworks. JUnit Jupiter provides the programming model and extension model for writing JUnit 5 tests. JUnit Vintage allows older JUnit 3 and JUnit 4 tests to run on the JUnit Platform during migration. ## Practical Example A basic Jupiter test uses `@Test` from `org.junit.jupiter.api.Test`: ```java import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test; import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertEquals; class CalculatorTest { @Test void addsTwoNumbers() { Calculator calculator = new Calculator(); assertEquals(5, calculator.add(2, 3)); } } ``` The test verifies observable behavior rather than implementation details. If the result differs from the expected value, JUnit reports a failure with the expected and actual values. ## DevOps Application A CI pipeline runs the test suite before packaging an application. A failing JUnit test should fail the Maven or Gradle test task and prevent an invalid build artifact from being promoted. ## Key Takeaway Use Jupiter for new tests, Platform-compatible launchers for execution, and Vintage only when legacy JUnit tests still need to run.

Heading: JUnit 5 Architecture — Framework Architecture
Content: # JUnit 5 Architecture — Framework Architecture ## Learning Objective Understand the three major JUnit 5 components and how they cooperate during test execution. ## Platform, Jupiter, and Vintage JUnit Platform is the launcher and test-engine infrastructure. It discovers test engines, selects tests, executes them, and publishes execution results. JUnit Jupiter is the engine and API for JUnit 5 tests, including annotations such as `@Test`, `@BeforeEach`, and `@ParameterizedTest`. JUnit Vintage is an optional engine for running JUnit 3 and JUnit 4 tests. ## Execution Flow A build tool or IDE starts the JUnit Platform launcher. The launcher discovers available test engines. The Jupiter engine discovers Jupiter test classes and methods, creates the required test instances, runs lifecycle callbacks, executes test methods, and reports results. ## Maven Configuration A Maven project normally uses `junit-jupiter` as a test dependency and a compatible Surefire version to execute tests: ```xml <dependency> <groupId>org.junit.jupiter</groupId> <artifactId>junit-jupiter</artifactId> <version>5.10.2</version> <scope>test</scope> </dependency> ``` Keep dependency and plugin versions controlled through the project build configuration. ## Troubleshooting If tests compile but are not discovered, verify the test engine dependency, Surefire version, test class naming, and package structure. Check `mvn test` output rather than assuming that a successful compilation means tests executed. ## Key Takeaway The Platform launches tests, Jupiter supplies the modern testing model, and Vintage supports legacy test migration.

Heading: JUnit 5 Architecture — Test Design and Implementation
Content: # JUnit 5 Architecture — Test Design and Implementation ## Learning Objective Create tests that verify business behavior, remain understandable, and detect regressions without depending on internal implementation details. ## Test Structure A well-designed test has three logical steps: arrange the required inputs and dependencies, act by invoking the behavior under test, and assert the observable result. Keep each test focused on one behavior or one clearly related set of outcomes. ## Example ```java @Test void rejectsNegativeQuantity() { OrderService service = new OrderService(); IllegalArgumentException error = assertThrows( IllegalArgumentException.class, () -> service.calculateTotal(-2, 100) ); assertEquals("Quantity must be positive", error.getMessage()); } ``` The test checks both the exception type and its meaningful message. It does not inspect private fields or rely on the order of internal method calls. ## Design Guidance Use descriptive names such as `rejectsNegativeQuantity`. Include boundary values, valid inputs, invalid inputs, and important business rules. Avoid tests that depend on current time, random values, shared mutable state, or external services unless those dependencies are controlled. ## DevOps Application Reliable tests provide fast feedback in pull requests. Small, deterministic tests make failures easier to diagnose and reduce unnecessary CI reruns. ## Key Takeaway Test externally visible behavior and make failures explain exactly which business rule was violated.

Heading: JUnit 5 Architecture — Assertions and Lifecycle
Content: # JUnit 5 Architecture — Assertions and Lifecycle ## Learning Objective Use JUnit assertions and lifecycle callbacks to control test setup, execution, and cleanup. ## Assertions JUnit Jupiter provides assertions including `assertEquals`, `assertTrue`, `assertFalse`, `assertNull`, `assertNotNull`, `assertThrows`, and `assertAll`. Assertions should express the expected behavior clearly. `assertAll` is useful when several independent properties should be checked together. ## Lifecycle Annotations `@BeforeEach` runs before each test method. `@AfterEach` runs after each test method. `@BeforeAll` and `@AfterAll` run once for the test class; by default, these methods must be static unless the test class uses `@TestInstance(TestInstance.Lifecycle.PER_CLASS)`. ## Example ```java class AccountTest { private Account account; @BeforeEach void setUp() { account = new Account(100); } @Test void withdrawReducesBalance() { account.withdraw(30); assertEquals(70, account.getBalance()); } @AfterEach void cleanUp() { account = null; } } ``` ## Common Mistakes Do not put test-specific state in static fields without a clear reason. Avoid relying on test execution order. Each test should be independently executable. ## Key Takeaway Use lifecycle callbacks for predictable setup and cleanup, and assertions for clear verification of outcomes.

Heading: JUnit 5 Architecture — Mocking and Dependency Isolation
Content: # JUnit 5 Architecture — Mocking and Dependency Isolation ## Learning Objective Understand why unit tests isolate external dependencies and how JUnit 5 works with mocking libraries such as Mockito. ## Dependency Isolation A unit test should normally exercise one unit of application behavior without requiring a real database, network service, message broker, or filesystem. Mockito can create mock collaborators whose responses are controlled by the test. ## Example with Mockito ```java @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) class PaymentServiceTest { @Mock PaymentGateway gateway; @InjectMocks PaymentService service; @Test void returnsApprovedWhenGatewayApproves() { when(gateway.charge(500)).thenReturn(true); boolean result = service.pay(500); assertTrue(result); verify(gateway).charge(500); } } ``` The Mockito extension initializes annotated mocks for each test context. The test configures the gateway response and verifies the service result and required interaction. ## Design Guidance Mock boundaries such as remote clients and repositories, not every object in the application. Excessive mocking can make tests verify implementation details instead of behavior. Use real simple domain objects where practical. ## Troubleshooting If a mock is unexpectedly null, check extension registration, annotation usage, and test initialization. If a stub is unused, verify that the code path actually calls the mocked method. ## Key Takeaway JUnit provides test execution and assertions; Mockito provides controlled test doubles for dependencies.

Heading: JUnit 5 Architecture — Unit and Integration Testing
Content: # JUnit 5 Architecture — Unit and Integration Testing ## Learning Objective Distinguish unit tests from integration tests and select the correct level for each requirement. ## Unit Tests A unit test checks a small component in isolation. It is usually fast and uses controlled collaborators. Examples include validating a calculation, checking input validation, or testing a business rule. ## Integration Tests An integration test verifies that multiple components work together. It may involve Spring application configuration, persistence, serialization, HTTP endpoints, or a real database instance. Integration tests are slower because they initialize more infrastructure. ## Example A unit test for a service can mock its repository. An integration test can start a Spring application context and verify that a repository query correctly persists and retrieves an entity. ## Test Selection Use unit tests for detailed business-rule coverage. Use integration tests for framework wiring, database mappings, transaction behavior, and communication between components. Do not use a large integration test for every small calculation. ## CI Pipeline Run fast unit tests early in pull-request validation. Run integration tests in a controlled environment with required services and collect their reports as build artifacts. ## Key Takeaway Unit tests isolate behavior; integration tests prove that collaborating components work together.

Heading: JUnit 5 Architecture — Container-Based Testing
Content: # JUnit 5 Architecture — Container-Based Testing ## Learning Objective Understand how JUnit tests can use containerized dependencies to verify application behavior against realistic infrastructure. ## Why Container-Based Tests Mocks cannot fully reproduce database SQL behavior, broker protocols, or service-specific configuration. Testcontainers can start disposable Docker containers for dependencies such as PostgreSQL, MySQL, Redis, and Kafka during automated tests. ## Example A Java test can declare a PostgreSQL container and use its connection details to configure a data source. The test then exercises repository operations against an actual PostgreSQL server rather than an in-memory substitute. ```java @Testcontainers class RepositoryIntegrationTest { @Container static PostgreSQLContainer<?> database = new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16-alpine"); } ``` Add the appropriate Testcontainers modules and configure the application to use the container's mapped port and credentials. ## Operational Requirements The test runner needs access to a Docker-compatible runtime. Pin container image versions, avoid relying on a developer-specific local database, and ensure containers are stopped after execution. ## CI Application A CI agent must provide Docker access or a supported container runtime. Capture logs when startup fails and distinguish infrastructure startup errors from application test failures. ## Key Takeaway Container-based tests provide realistic dependency behavior while keeping test infrastructure disposable and repeatable.

Heading: JUnit 5 Architecture — Coverage and Quality Measurement
Content: # JUnit 5 Architecture — Coverage and Quality Measurement ## Learning Objective Measure which parts of application code are exercised by tests and understand the limitations of coverage metrics. ## Coverage Types Line coverage measures executed source lines. Branch coverage measures whether decision outcomes have been exercised. Instruction and method coverage provide additional views depending on the coverage tool. ## JaCoCo Integration JaCoCo instruments Java execution and produces coverage data that can be converted into HTML and XML reports. Maven projects commonly use the JaCoCo Maven plugin to prepare the agent, run tests, and generate a report. ## Quality Interpretation High coverage does not guarantee correct tests. A test may execute a line without asserting meaningful behavior. Focus on critical business branches, error handling, security checks, and boundary conditions rather than chasing a percentage alone. ## CI Enforcement A pipeline can publish the JaCoCo report and apply a minimum coverage rule. Configure thresholds carefully and review exclusions so generated code or irrelevant packages do not distort results. ## Troubleshooting If the report is empty, verify that tests ran with the JaCoCo agent and that the report goal reads the execution data from the expected location. ## Key Takeaway Use coverage to identify untested code, then assess whether tests contain meaningful assertions.

Heading: JUnit 5 Architecture — Test Reporting
Content: # JUnit 5 Architecture — Test Reporting ## Learning Objective Interpret JUnit test results and publish useful reports for developers and CI systems. ## Result Categories A test can pass, fail because an assertion was not satisfied, or abort because execution could not continue. Build tools also report errors caused by test initialization, compilation, dependency resolution, or test-engine failures. These conditions should not be treated as identical. ## Maven Reports Maven Surefire executes unit tests and writes XML and text reports under `target/surefire-reports`. Failsafe commonly handles integration tests and writes reports under `target/failsafe-reports`. ## Investigation Start with the failed test name and stack trace. Identify the assertion, exception, or setup failure. Compare the failing run with the previous successful build and inspect relevant application logs. ## CI Integration Archive test reports even when the test step fails. This allows developers to inspect failures after the pipeline has stopped. Configure the CI platform to display JUnit-compatible XML results when supported. ## Key Takeaway A useful report identifies the exact failing test, preserves diagnostic details, and remains available after a failed pipeline.

Heading: JUnit 5 Architecture — Flaky Test Investigation
Content: # JUnit 5 Architecture — Flaky Test Investigation ## Learning Objective Identify tests that pass and fail without a relevant code change and remove the underlying source of nondeterminism. ## Common Causes Flaky tests often depend on timing, shared mutable state, test execution order, random input, external network services, machine load, or incomplete cleanup. Parallel execution can expose hidden shared-state problems. ## Investigation Process Record the failing test name, seed, environment, execution duration, and stack trace. Re-run the individual test, then run it repeatedly and with the full suite. Compare isolated and parallel execution to determine whether the failure is caused by shared resources or order dependence. ## JUnit Controls Use `@BeforeEach` and `@AfterEach` to create and clean test state. Avoid arbitrary sleeps. Prefer waiting for a specific condition with a bounded timeout when asynchronous behavior must be tested. Use `@ResourceLock` when tests genuinely share a resource and parallel execution is enabled. ## CI Response Do not permanently hide flaky tests by adding unlimited retries. Track failure frequency, assign ownership, and fix the source. A temporary quarantine should be visible and time-limited. ## Key Takeaway A flaky test is a reliability defect in the test suite. Find the nondeterministic dependency instead of repeatedly rerunning the pipeline.

Heading: JUnit 5 Architecture — CI Integration
Content: # JUnit 5 Architecture — CI Integration ## Learning Objective Execute JUnit tests consistently in continuous integration and make test failures visible to the development team. ## Maven Execution A typical Maven validation command is: ```bash mvn -B clean verify ``` The `test` phase runs unit tests through Surefire. When Failsafe is configured, integration tests run during the integration-test phase and are checked during the verify phase. ## Pipeline Design Use a clean checkout, install the required JDK, resolve dependencies, compile source code, execute tests, and publish reports. Cache Maven dependencies where appropriate, but do not reuse stale build output as a substitute for a clean validation run. ## Example Jenkins Stage ```groovy stage('Test') { steps { sh 'mvn -B clean verify' } post { always { junit testResults: '**/target/*-reports/TEST-*.xml', allowEmptyResults: true } } } ``` Adjust report patterns to match the project's actual Surefire and Failsafe output locations. ## Failure Handling A non-zero Maven exit code should fail the pipeline. Preserve XML reports and logs so developers can diagnose the failure. Do not mark a build successful merely because report publishing completed. ## Key Takeaway CI must execute the real test lifecycle, fail on test failures, and retain reports for investigation.

Heading: JUnit 5 Architecture — Production Test Strategy
Content: # JUnit 5 Architecture — Production Test Strategy ## Learning Objective Design a layered test strategy that provides fast feedback while protecting critical application behavior before release. ## Test Layers Use unit tests for business rules and edge cases. Use integration tests for persistence, framework wiring, and service collaboration. Use API or end-to-end tests for critical user workflows. Keep the broadest tests smaller in number because they require more infrastructure and are usually slower. ## Risk-Based Coverage Prioritize payment calculations, authorization, data validation, transaction boundaries, failure handling, and backward compatibility. Test both successful and rejected operations. Include regression tests whenever a production defect is fixed. ## Reliability Tests should be deterministic, isolated, repeatable, and safe to run concurrently where possible. External dependencies should be controlled through mocks for unit tests or disposable infrastructure for integration tests. ## Release Pipeline Require compilation, unit tests, integration tests, static analysis, and relevant security checks before artifact promotion. Store test reports and associate them with the exact commit and build artifact. ## Production Feedback Monitor escaped defects and add regression tests for failures found after deployment. A test suite should evolve with incidents and changing business requirements. ## Key Takeaway A production test strategy balances speed, realism, risk coverage, and repeatability instead of relying on one large test suite.

Heading: JUnit 5 Architecture — Hands-on Testing Exercise
Content: # JUnit 5 Architecture — Hands-on Testing Exercise ## Objective Build and execute a small JUnit Jupiter test suite for a Java calculator service. ## Implementation Create a `Calculator` class with `add`, `subtract`, and `divide` methods. Define expected behavior for normal inputs and division by zero. Keep business logic separate from the test class. ## Test Cases Write Jupiter tests that verify positive and negative addition, subtraction, division with a non-zero divisor, and the expected exception for division by zero. Use descriptive test names and assertions such as `assertEquals` and `assertThrows`. ## Execute Run the project tests using: ```bash mvn test ``` Inspect the Maven output and the XML reports under `target/surefire-reports`. ## Failure Exercise Temporarily change the expected result in one test. Run the tests again and identify the failed assertion, expected value, actual value, and non-zero build status. Restore the correct expectation after observing the failure. ## Completion Criteria All tests pass, the test report contains the expected test cases, and the test suite can run repeatedly without depending on execution order or external infrastructure. ## Key Takeaway A useful exercise proves both the successful path and the failure-reporting behavior of the build.

Heading: JUnit 5 Architecture — Testing Strategy and Fundamentals — JUnit 5 Architecture [stage-5-topic-2-section-14]
Content: # JUnit 5 Architecture — Migration and Compatibility ## Learning Objective Understand how a Java project can migrate from JUnit 4 to JUnit Jupiter while keeping legacy tests executable during the transition. ## Compatibility Model JUnit Vintage is the test engine for running JUnit 3 and JUnit 4 tests on the JUnit Platform. It is optional and should be retained only while the project still has legacy tests. JUnit Jupiter is the recommended programming model for new JUnit 5 tests. ## Migration Considerations JUnit 4 uses annotations such as `org.junit.Test` and `org.junit.Before`. Jupiter uses `org.junit.jupiter.api.Test` and `org.junit.jupiter.api.BeforeEach`. Imports must be updated carefully; identical annotation names from different packages are not interchangeable. ## Build Configuration Add Jupiter dependencies and a compatible Surefire plugin. If legacy tests remain, include the Vintage engine as a test-scoped dependency. Remove Vintage after all legacy tests have been migrated and validated. ## Validation Run the complete test suite before and after migration. Compare discovered test counts, failures, skipped tests, and report output. Pay special attention to lifecycle behavior, rules, runners, and parameterized tests because migration may require design changes. ## Key Takeaway Migrate incrementally, run old and new tests through the Platform where needed, and remove compatibility components only after legacy tests are gone.

Confirm the current Kubernetes context with kubectl config current-context. 2. Select and verify the correct namespace. 3. Inspect the relevant resources before changing anything. 4. Review the manifest fields, image reference, labels, selectors, resources, and permissions. 5. Apply the required configuration using a reviewed manifest or approved deployment process. 6. Observe controller reconciliation and Pod scheduling. 7. Inspect Pod conditions, container state, events, and logs. 8. Verify networking, storage, and application readiness where required. 9. Record the manifest revision, image digest, and resulting workload state. Use namespaces and explicit resource names to avoid changing the wrong environment.
