Cover dependency declarations, version constraints, package retrieval, repository authentication where applicable, artifact integrity, and reproducibility. Explain how a team should pin versions, update dependencies deliberately, validate downloaded packages, and prevent an uncontrolled dependency change from affecting production releases. The engineering area covered by this section is Argo CD GitOps continuous delivery. The purpose is to understand how the relevant mechanism works, which configuration controls it, and how its behavior affects a Kubernetes application delivery workflow. ### 2. Core technical concepts Argo CD is a declarative GitOps continuous delivery tool for Kubernetes. It continuously observes application configuration stored in Git or another supported source and compares that desired configuration with the live resources in a target cluster. An Argo CD Application resource describes the source repository, path or chart, destination cluster and namespace, and synchronization behavior. Argo CD separates the desired state stored in source control from the live state running in Kubernetes. Its application controller compares these states and reports synchronization and health information. Depending on configuration and permissions, synchronization can apply changes to the target cluster. Self-healing can correct certain live-state modifications by reconciling resources back toward the declared desired state. A DevOps engineer should distinguish the desired configuration from the actual state. Configuration describes what should exist; the deployment or reconciliation system processes that configuration; Kubernetes controllers and application components determine the eventual runtime behavior. These are related but separate stages. ### 3. Internal processing and workflow A typical GitOps workflow starts when an engineer changes Kubernetes manifests, Helm values, or another supported deployment source and commits the change to Git. Argo CD detects the updated revision, renders or generates the desired resources, compares them with live cluster resources, and reports the difference. An authorized synchronization operation applies the desired resources. The application controller then observes the resulting state and updates application health and synchronization status. Git is the auditable source of desired configuration. Direct changes made to the cluster can create drift because they are not represented in the repository. The correct remediation is normally to review and correct the source configuration rather than repeatedly editing live resources. For this particular section, identify the input configuration, the component that processes it, the resulting Kubernetes resources, and the evidence that confirms successful execution. Follow the operation from its source through validation and processing to the target cluster. Do not assume that a successful package operation, Git commit, synchronization request, or API response guarantees a healthy application. Confirm the resulting Kubernetes resource state and application behavior independently. ### 4. Practical commands The following commands are relevant starting points for investigating this subject. Replace placeholder names with actual release names, application names, chart paths, and namespaces. argocd repo list argocd account get-user-info argocd account can-i get applications kubectl get secrets -n argocd kubectl get roles,rolebindings -n argocd ### 5. Configuration and implementation considerations When implementing this capability, keep configuration version-controlled and review changes before deployment. Use explicit versions for charts and dependencies. Keep credentials out of source files and command history. Validate rendered manifests before they reach a production cluster. For Helm-based deployments, review the chart package, values, rendered resources, and release history. For Argo CD-based delivery, review the source revision, destination, Application configuration, project policy, synchronization settings, and resulting resource state. ### 6. Verification and operational evidence Verify the Application source revision, destination cluster and namespace, synchronization status, health status, and resource tree. Inspect the generated manifests and compare them with live resources. Confirm that the destination workload is healthy through Kubernetes conditions, Pod readiness, Service connectivity, and application-level checks. A Synced status alone does not prove application availability. Useful evidence includes the source commit or chart version, rendered manifests, deployment command or synchronization record, Kubernetes events, controller status, Pod conditions, application logs, and relevant monitoring signals. Capture evidence before changing a failing release so the original failure can be investigated accurately. ### 7. Troubleshooting approach If the operation fails, isolate the failure layer before applying a correction. - Check whether the source repository or chart package can be accessed. - Validate chart metadata, dependencies, values, templates, or manifest generation. - Confirm that the correct cluster, namespace, and target revision are selected. - Check credentials and authorization separately. - Inspect Kubernetes API responses and resource events. - Check whether controllers created the expected resources. - Inspect Pod scheduling, image retrieval, startup, probes, and application logs. - Confirm the resulting state after remediation. Avoid deleting releases, pruning resources, or manually editing production objects as an initial troubleshooting step. Understand ownership and data impact first. ### 8. CI/CD and GitOps integration A mature pipeline should validate source changes before deployment. For Helm, this includes chart linting, dependency validation, template rendering, manifest review, and controlled release promotion. For Argo CD, it includes pull-request review, repository validation, Application policy checks, controlled synchronization, and post-deployment health verification. Keep application image versions separate from chart versions. Promote the same tested image digest through environments. Record the source commit, chart version, configuration revision, target environment, and deployment result so that every release can be traced and audited. ### 9. Security and production practices Protect Argo CD using SSO or another approved authentication mechanism, narrowly scoped RBAC policies, repository credentials stored through supported secure mechanisms, and controlled destination-cluster permissions. Avoid broad administrator access for routine application operations. Review who can modify repositories, Application resources, project policies, and synchronization settings. Do not expose repository tokens or private keys in logs, Git files, or terminal output. Use separate permissions for development and production, protect deployment credentials, review changes to synchronization and pruning settings, and restrict who can modify deployment sources. Monitor release failures, application health, synchronization delays, and unexpected live-state changes. ### 10. Practical engineer checklist - Confirm the correct repository, chart or application, and version. - Review configuration and environment-specific values. - Validate templates or generated manifests. - Confirm destination cluster and namespace. - Check credentials and least-privilege permissions. - Review the expected resource changes before applying them. - Monitor the release or synchronization operation. - Verify Kubernetes workload and application health. - Record the source revision and deployment evidence. - Document the root cause and recovery steps for failures.

Content: ## Observability Fundamentals — Observability and Monitoring Fundamentals ### 1. Technical explanation Explain 'Observability Fundamentals — Observability and Monitoring Fundamentals' as a distinct technical subject within 'Observability Fundamentals'. Cover its definition, purpose, internal mechanism, configuration, data flow, dependencies, practical implementation, verification, common failure modes, performance implications, and production operating practices. The engineering area is Observability Fundamentals. Understand the exact operational problem addressed by this section, the data involved, the responsible components, and the decision an engineer must make using this capability. Monitoring is useful only when its measurements represent real system behavior and can be interpreted correctly. ### 2. Core concepts Observability connects metrics, logs, and traces to explain system behavior. Metrics show numerical trends, logs preserve individual events, and traces show request journeys across distributed components. Monitoring uses these signals to detect known conditions and evaluate service health. The concepts above provide the foundation for this section. Apply them to the specific behavior described by 'Observability Fundamentals — Observability and Monitoring Fundamentals'. Identify the inputs, outputs, configuration, dependencies, and expected operational result. Distinguish the monitoring component's own health from the health of the application or infrastructure it observes. ### 3. Internal workflow Trace the complete process from the original measurement to the component that consumes it. Identify which application or system generates the signal, which endpoint exposes it, which component collects or queries it, where it is stored, and which dashboard or alert uses it. When a signal is missing, investigate each boundary separately. A working application does not guarantee a working exporter, and a healthy exporter does not guarantee that Prometheus has successfully scraped its metrics. Similarly, a successful scrape does not guarantee that a dashboard query selects the correct series. ### 4. Practical commands Use the following commands as investigation starting points. Adjust hostnames, ports, file paths, credentials, and query expressions to match the environment. promtool check config prometheus.yml curl http://localhost:9090/-/healthy curl http://localhost:9090/-/ready curl http://localhost:9090/api/v1/targets curl http://localhost:9090/api/v1/status/config Check command output and service responses rather than assuming success. Protect credentials and avoid exposing passwords, tokens, or private configuration in shell history or shared logs. ### 5. Implementation and configuration Configure this capability with consistent naming, documented units, useful labels, suitable collection intervals, and controlled configuration changes. Validate configuration before reloading monitoring services. Keep scrape jobs, rule files, alert routes, and dashboard definitions under version control. Configuration should solve a defined operational requirement. Review expected sample volume, label cardinality, query load, storage retention, and dashboard refresh frequency. Excessive collection and unbounded label values can increase monitoring cost without improving incident detection. ### 6. Verification and acceptance criteria Verify the source endpoint, target discovery, scrape status, metric freshness, query result, and relevant component health. Check application and exporter logs, Prometheus target state, configuration reload status, and recent monitoring events. Compare the monitoring output with actual service behavior. For production acceptance, verify that the configuration is version-controlled, access is restricted, credentials are protected, and operational ownership is documented. Test failure scenarios in a controlled environment and confirm that monitoring identifies the condition without generating misleading alerts. A successful implementation should provide fresh and correctly interpreted measurements. Confirm that queries return expected values, labels identify the correct target, and dashboards show the intended time range. Where alerting is involved, test the complete notification path using a controlled condition. ### 7. Troubleshooting workflow Investigate the signal in sequence: 1. Confirm that the application or system generates the expected measurement. 2. Verify that the exporter or metrics endpoint is reachable. 3. Inspect Prometheus target discovery and scrape status. 4. Check metric names, labels, timestamps, and query results. 5. Validate configuration and rule evaluation status. 6. Inspect Alertmanager routing and notification errors where relevant. 7. Verify Grafana data-source health and panel queries. 8. Compare monitoring evidence with application logs and actual service behavior. Separate an application incident from a monitoring pipeline failure. A missing metric may indicate an unavailable service, but it may also result from a broken exporter, incorrect discovery rule, scrape timeout, or query filter. ### 8. DevOps and CI/CD integration Store monitoring configuration in version control. CI pipelines can validate Prometheus configuration with promtool, validate rule files, run query checks, and review Grafana dashboard definitions before promotion. Deploy monitoring configuration through a controlled workflow with change history and rollback procedures. Use consistent labels for service, environment, cluster, namespace, and team ownership. This makes dashboards, alerts, and incident investigations consistent across development, staging, and production. ### 9. Production security and reliability Protect monitoring endpoints, dashboard access, data-source credentials, and alert receivers. Restrict access to sensitive infrastructure metrics and avoid exposing internal endpoints publicly. Apply retention and capacity policies based on actual operational requirements. Monitor the monitoring stack itself. Track scrape failures, target availability, ingestion pressure, storage capacity, query latency, rule-evaluation delays, alert delivery failures, and Grafana availability. Monitoring must remain useful during the incidents it is designed to detect. ### 10. Technical explanation For 'Exporters — Recording and Alert Rules', explain the source of measurements, collection method, exporter responsibilities, HTTP endpoint, required permissions, and Prometheus scrape behavior. Distinguish exporter availability from successful metric ingestion. The engineering area is Exporters. Understand the exact operational problem addressed by this section, the data involved, the responsible components, and the decision an engineer must make using this capability. Monitoring is useful only when its measurements represent real system behavior and can be interpreted correctly. ### 2. Core concepts Exporters expose measurements from systems that do not natively provide Prometheus metrics. Node Exporter exposes host metrics, Blackbox Exporter performs network probes, and application-specific exporters collect database or infrastructure measurements. Prometheus scrapes exporter HTTP endpoints and stores the returned time series. The concepts above provide the foundation for this section. Apply them to the specific behavior described by 'Exporters — Recording and Alert Rules'. Identify the inputs, outputs, configuration, dependencies, and expected operational result. Distinguish the monitoring component's own health from the health of the application or infrastructure it observes. ### 3. Internal workflow Trace the complete process from the original measurement to the component that consumes it. Identify which application or system generates the signal, which endpoint exposes it, which component collects or queries it, where it is stored, and which dashboard or alert uses it. When a signal is missing, investigate each boundary separately. A working application does not guarantee a working exporter, and a healthy exporter does not guarantee that Prometheus has successfully scraped its metrics. Similarly, a successful scrape does not guarantee that a dashboard query selects the correct series. ### 4. Practical commands Use the following commands as investigation starting points. Adjust hostnames, ports, file paths, credentials, and query expressions to match the environment. curl http://localhost:9100/metrics curl http://localhost:9115/metrics curl http://localhost:9090/api/v1/targets Check command output and service responses rather than assuming success. Protect credentials and avoid exposing passwords, tokens, or private configuration in shell history or shared logs. ### 5. Implementation and configuration Configure this capability with consistent naming, documented units, useful labels, suitable collection intervals, and controlled configuration changes. Validate configuration before reloading monitoring services. Keep scrape jobs, rule files, alert routes, and dashboard definitions under version control. Configuration should solve a defined operational requirement. Review expected sample volume, label cardinality, query load, storage retention, and dashboard refresh frequency. Excessive collection and unbounded label values can increase monitoring cost without improving incident detection. ### 6. Verification and acceptance criteria Verify the source endpoint, target discovery, scrape status, metric freshness, query result, and relevant component health. Check application and exporter logs, Prometheus target state, configuration reload status, and recent monitoring events. Compare the monitoring output with actual service behavior. For production acceptance, verify that the configuration is version-controlled, access is restricted, credentials are protected, and operational ownership is documented. Test failure scenarios in a controlled environment and confirm that monitoring identifies the condition without generating misleading alerts. A successful implementation should provide fresh and correctly interpreted measurements. Confirm that queries return expected values, labels identify the correct target, and dashboards show the intended time range. Where alerting is involved, test the complete notification path using a controlled condition. ### 7. Troubleshooting workflow Investigate the signal in sequence: 1. Confirm that the application or system generates the expected measurement. 2. Verify that the exporter or metrics endpoint is reachable. 3. Inspect Prometheus target discovery and scrape status. 4. Check metric names, labels, timestamps, and query results. 5. Validate configuration and rule evaluation status. 6. Inspect Alertmanager routing and notification errors where relevant. 7. Verify Grafana data-source health and panel queries. 8. Compare monitoring evidence with application logs and actual service behavior. Separate an application incident from a monitoring pipeline failure. A missing metric may indicate an unavailable service, but it may also result from a broken exporter, incorrect discovery rule, scrape timeout, or query filter. ### 8. DevOps and CI/CD integration Store monitoring configuration in version control. CI pipelines can validate Prometheus configuration with promtool, validate rule files, run query checks, and review Grafana dashboard definitions before promotion. Deploy monitoring configuration through a controlled workflow with change history and rollback procedures. Use consistent labels for service, environment, cluster, namespace, and team ownership. This makes dashboards, alerts, and incident investigations consistent across development, staging, and production. ### 9. Production security and reliability Protect monitoring endpoints, dashboard access, data-source credentials, and alert receivers. Restrict access to sensitive infrastructure metrics and avoid exposing internal endpoints publicly. Apply retention and capacity policies based on actual operational requirements. Monitor the monitoring stack itself. Track scrape failures, target availability, ingestion pressure, storage capacity, query latency, rule-evaluation delays, alert delivery failures, and Grafana availability. Monitoring must remain useful during the incidents it is designed to detect. ### 10. Practical engineering checklist - Identify the operational question this feature must answer. - Confirm the source system and metric semantics. - Validate collection, discovery, and configuration. - Check labels, units, and cardinality. - Test queries with realistic time windows. - Verify dashboards and alert behavior. - Protect credentials and monitoring endpoints. - Monitor the monitoring platform's own health. - Document the signal owner and investigation procedure.

Technical explanation For 'Alert Rules — Exporters and Service Discovery', explain the source of measurements, collection method, exporter responsibilities, HTTP endpoint, required permissions, and Prometheus scrape behavior. Distinguish exporter availability from successful metric ingestion. The engineering area is Alert Rules. Understand the exact operational problem addressed by this section, the data involved, the responsible components, and the decision an engineer must make using this capability. Monitoring is useful only when its measurements represent real system behavior and can be interpreted correctly. ### 2. Core concepts Prometheus alert rules evaluate PromQL conditions and create alert instances. The for duration requires a condition to remain active before firing. Labels identify the affected service and severity, while annotations provide summaries and investigation links. Alerts should be actionable and connected to a response owner. The concepts above provide the foundation for this section. Apply them to the specific behavior described by 'Alert Rules — Exporters and Service Discovery'. Identify the inputs, outputs, configuration, dependencies, and expected operational result. Distinguish the monitoring component's own health from the health of the application or infrastructure it observes. ### 3. Internal workflow Trace the complete process from the original measurement to the component that consumes it. Identify which application or system generates the signal, which endpoint exposes it, which component collects or queries it, where it is stored, and which dashboard or alert uses it. When a signal is missing, investigate each boundary separately. A working application does not guarantee a working exporter, and a healthy exporter does not guarantee that Prometheus has successfully scraped its metrics. Similarly, a successful scrape does not guarantee that a dashboard query selects the correct series. ### 4. Practical commands Use the following commands as investigation starting points. Adjust hostnames, ports, file paths, credentials, and query expressions to match the environment. promtool check rules rules.yml curl http://localhost:9090/api/v1/rules curl http://localhost:9090/api/v1/alerts Check command output and service responses rather than assuming success. Protect credentials and avoid exposing passwords, tokens, or private configuration in shell history or shared logs. ### 5. Implementation and configuration Configure this capability with consistent naming, documented units, useful labels, suitable collection intervals, and controlled configuration changes. Validate configuration before reloading monitoring services. Keep scrape jobs, rule files, alert routes, and dashboard definitions under version control. Configuration should solve a defined operational requirement. Review expected sample volume, label cardinality, query load, storage retention, and dashboard refresh frequency. Excessive collection and unbounded label values can increase monitoring cost without improving incident detection. ### 6. Verification and acceptance criteria Verify the source endpoint, target discovery, scrape status, metric freshness, query result, and relevant component health. Check application and exporter logs, Prometheus target state, configuration reload status, and recent monitoring events. Compare the monitoring output with actual service behavior. For production acceptance, verify that the configuration is version-controlled, access is restricted, credentials are protected, and operational ownership is documented. Test failure scenarios in a controlled environment and confirm that monitoring identifies the condition without generating misleading alerts. A successful implementation should provide fresh and correctly interpreted measurements. Confirm that queries return expected values, labels identify the correct target, and dashboards show the intended time range. Where alerting is involved, test the complete notification path using a controlled condition. ### 7. Troubleshooting workflow Investigate the signal in sequence: 1. Confirm that the application or system generates the expected measurement. 2. Verify that the exporter or metrics endpoint is reachable. 3. Inspect Prometheus target discovery and scrape status. 4. Check metric names, labels, timestamps, and query results. 5. Validate configuration and rule evaluation status. 6. Inspect Alertmanager routing and notification errors where relevant. 7. Verify Grafana data-source health and panel queries. 8. Compare monitoring evidence with application logs and actual service behavior. Separate an application incident from a monitoring pipeline failure. A missing metric may indicate an unavailable service, but it may also result from a broken exporter, incorrect discovery rule, scrape timeout, or query filter. ### 8. DevOps and CI/CD integration Store monitoring configuration in version control. CI pipelines can validate Prometheus configuration with promtool, validate rule files, run query checks, and review Grafana dashboard definitions before promotion. Deploy monitoring configuration through a controlled workflow with change history and rollback procedures. Use consistent labels for service, environment, cluster, namespace, and team ownership. This makes dashboards, alerts, and incident investigations consistent across development, staging, and production. ### 9. Production security and reliability Protect monitoring endpoints, dashboard access, data-source credentials, and alert receivers. Restrict access to sensitive infrastructure metrics and avoid exposing internal endpoints publicly. Apply retention and capacity policies based on actual operational requirements. Monitor the monitoring stack itself. Track scrape failures, target availability, ingestion pressure, storage capacity, query latency, rule-evaluation delays, alert delivery failures, and Grafana availability. Monitoring must remain useful during the incidents it is designed to detect. ### 10. Technical explanation For 'Troubleshooting — Production Monitoring Strategy', explain metric selectors, label matchers, instant and range vectors, time windows, functions, aggregation, counter resets, and missing samples. Explain how to test the expression and verify that its result answers the intended operational question. The engineering area is Troubleshooting. Understand the exact operational problem addressed by this section, the data involved, the responsible components, and the decision an engineer must make using this capability. Monitoring is useful only when its measurements represent real system behavior and can be interpreted correctly. ### 2. Core concepts Monitoring failures can occur in instrumentation, exporters, networking, discovery, scraping, storage, queries, rules, dashboards, or notification delivery. Troubleshooting should follow the telemetry path and inspect evidence at each layer rather than assuming that an empty dashboard means the application is down. The concepts above provide the foundation for this section. Apply them to the specific behavior described by 'Troubleshooting — Production Monitoring Strategy'. Identify the inputs, outputs, configuration, dependencies, and expected operational result. Distinguish the monitoring component's own health from the health of the application or infrastructure it observes. ### 3. Internal workflow Trace the complete process from the original measurement to the component that consumes it. Identify which application or system generates the signal, which endpoint exposes it, which component collects or queries it, where it is stored, and which dashboard or alert uses it. When a signal is missing, investigate each boundary separately. A working application does not guarantee a working exporter, and a healthy exporter does not guarantee that Prometheus has successfully scraped its metrics. Similarly, a successful scrape does not guarantee that a dashboard query selects the correct series. ### 4. Practical commands Use the following commands as investigation starting points. Adjust hostnames, ports, file paths, credentials, and query expressions to match the environment. promtool check config prometheus.yml curl http://localhost:9090/-/healthy curl http://localhost:9090/-/ready curl http://localhost:9090/api/v1/targets curl http://localhost:9090/api/v1/status/config Check command output and service responses rather than assuming success. Protect credentials and avoid exposing passwords, tokens, or private configuration in shell history or shared logs. ### 5. Implementation and configuration Configure this capability with consistent naming, documented units, useful labels, suitable collection intervals, and controlled configuration changes. Validate configuration before reloading monitoring services. Keep scrape jobs, rule files, alert routes, and dashboard definitions under version control. Configuration should solve a defined operational requirement. Review expected sample volume, label cardinality, query load, storage retention, and dashboard refresh frequency. Excessive collection and unbounded label values can increase monitoring cost without improving incident detection. ### 6. Verification and acceptance criteria Verify the source endpoint, target discovery, scrape status, metric freshness, query result, and relevant component health. Check application and exporter logs, Prometheus target state, configuration reload status, and recent monitoring events. Compare the monitoring output with actual service behavior. For production acceptance, verify that the configuration is version-controlled, access is restricted, credentials are protected, and operational ownership is documented. Test failure scenarios in a controlled environment and confirm that monitoring identifies the condition without generating misleading alerts. A successful implementation should provide fresh and correctly interpreted measurements. Confirm that queries return expected values, labels identify the correct target, and dashboards show the intended time range. Where alerting is involved, test the complete notification path using a controlled condition. ### 7. Troubleshooting workflow Investigate the signal in sequence: 1. Confirm that the application or system generates the expected measurement. 2. Verify that the exporter or metrics endpoint is reachable. 3. Inspect Prometheus target discovery and scrape status. 4. Check metric names, labels, timestamps, and query results. 5. Validate configuration and rule evaluation status. 6. Inspect Alertmanager routing and notification errors where relevant. 7. Verify Grafana data-source health and panel queries. 8. Compare monitoring evidence with application logs and actual service behavior. Separate an application incident from a monitoring pipeline failure. A missing metric may indicate an unavailable service, but it may also result from a broken exporter, incorrect discovery rule, scrape timeout, or query filter. ### 8. DevOps and CI/CD integration Store monitoring configuration in version control. CI pipelines can validate Prometheus configuration with promtool, validate rule files, run query checks, and review Grafana dashboard definitions before promotion. Deploy monitoring configuration through a controlled workflow with change history and rollback procedures. Use consistent labels for service, environment, cluster, namespace, and team ownership. This makes dashboards, alerts, and incident investigations consistent across development, staging, and production. ### 9. Production security and reliability Protect monitoring endpoints, dashboard access, data-source credentials, and alert receivers. Restrict access to sensitive infrastructure metrics and avoid exposing internal endpoints publicly. Apply retention and capacity policies based on actual operational requirements. Monitor the monitoring stack itself. Track scrape failures, target availability, ingestion pressure, storage capacity, query latency, rule-evaluation delays, alert delivery failures, and Grafana availability. Monitoring must remain useful during the incidents it is designed to detect. ### 10. Practical engineering checklist - Identify the operational question this feature must answer. - Confirm the source system and metric semantics. - Validate collection, discovery, and configuration. - Check labels, units, and cardinality. - Test queries with realistic time windows. - Verify dashboards and alert behavior. - Protect credentials and monitoring endpoints. - Monitor the monitoring platform's own health. - Document the signal owner and investigation procedure.
